paras: The threatened lynching of James Hayes occurred in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in late August 1903, after Hayes, a Black man who worked at a Minneapolis barn, was arrested on a charge of carrying 13-year-old Ruby Steele from her bedroom and attempting to assault her. Talk of lynching was reported and police guarded him and moved him to the county jail, but no mob formed. The case drew attention in both the white dailies and the Black weeklies of the Twin Cities, where a mass meeting of Black residents and the resolutions it adopted became a subject of dispute.

According to the Minneapolis Journal, an intruder entered the Steele home at 1414 Sixth street SE about 1 a.m. on Monday, August 24, held a chloroformed handkerchief over the girl's face, struck her mother down, and carried the girl to a nearby barn before neighbors drove him off. Detectives traced a handkerchief found in the room to Hayes's employer, F. A. Benjamin, and arrested Hayes when he returned to the Benjamin barn shortly before 6 a.m. Hayes denied the charge and said he had spent the night in St. Paul.

The Journal reported the same day that "Feeling is high" and that the police would guard the central station with an extra detail. The Saint Paul Globe wrote that talk of lynching "was frequently heard during the day," though no demonstration had been made by early the next morning. The police had already moved Hayes to the county jail that afternoon "to prevent every possibility of lynching," and, contrary to their expectation, no mob formed that night.

Black residents of Minneapolis called a mass meeting at the Knights of Pythias hall, demanding that Hayes be punished if guilty and protected until trial. By August 26 the Globe reported that feeling had changed, that Hayes's friends had sent to St. Paul for attorney F. L. McGhee, and that the excitement had died down.

At the preliminary hearing on August 29 the Journal found the state's case weak because of disagreements between the girl's and her mother's testimony, and the charge was reduced by stipulation to second-degree assault. Hayes was later indicted on three counts, and the county attorney chose to try him for first-degree burglary because that charge allowed a heavier sentence. Opposing a continuance, County Attorney Boardman told the court that delays had "caused the atrocities which have shocked the nation in the past months."

A jury convicted Hayes of first-degree burglary after about an hour, and on September 26 Judge C. M. Pond sentenced him to 25 years at hard labor in the Stillwater prison. At sentencing, defense attorney James L. Curtiss said the jury had found Hayes guilty and that he should be punished accordingly.

The white press first framed the case around the threat of lynching, with the Globe headlining that Hayes "May Be Lynched" and a wire item in Iowa running under "Would Lynch Girl's Assailer." The Journal called the attempt among the most atrocious in the city's history and described Hayes in derogatory physical terms, while country weeklies ran a digest item titled "A Negro Fiend." The same dailies later reported doubts, the Globe noting a disposition to suspend judgment and the Journal the weakness of the state's case.

In the Black press, the St. Paul Appeal reported the Twin Cities' excitement and "the feeling that there would be some mob volence," printed the mass meeting's resolution condemning the crime, and observed in its Minneapolis column that there were "two sides to the story." The Northwestern Vine attacked the resolution as prejudging Hayes, said residents had been driven to it by "negro-hating newspapers," and reported that attorney Curtiss had objected and been outvoted. Vine staff also interviewed the girl and her mother and printed their account, including the girl's statement that she was larger than Hayes.

Accounts differed on details of the alleged crime: the Journal said the intruder climbed onto a summer-kitchen roof, while the Vine's interview and the Globe's trial report said he used a ladder. Most papers gave Ruby Steele's age as 13, but the Appeal gave it as 14 and later as "more than fourteen."

framing.detail: The Minneapolis Journal called the attempt 'one of the most atrocious in the history of the city' and described Hayes in derogatory physical terms, yet days later reported the 'weakness of the case of the state'.
The Saint Paul Globe headlined that Hayes 'May Be Lynched' but noted a 'disposition in most quarters to suspend judgment' and then that feeling against him had changed.
Out-of-state and country papers ran wire or digest items headed 'Would Lynch Girl's Assailer' and 'A Negro Fiend'.
The St. Paul Appeal printed the mass meeting's resolution condemning the crime while its Minneapolis column said there were 'two sides to the story'.
The Northwestern Vine condemned the resolutions as prejudging Hayes and blamed 'negro-hating newspapers' for driving Black residents to adopt them.
